chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutevakil (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ali al-Kufy and Muhammad ibn al-Hussein, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Hamad al-Harithi, on the authority of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Five [people] whose supplication is not answered: A man whose wife bothers him and he does not divorce her, even though he has the means to provide for her and has not freed her path [from him]; A man whose slave has escaped three times, but he does not sell him; A man who passes by a leaning wall and it is falling towards him, but he does not hurry his walking until it falls upon him; A man who lends money to another but does not take a witness for it; And a man who sits in his house and says, 'O God, grant me sustenance,' but does not go out to seek it.
ai.seo_question: Who are the five people whose prayers are not answered according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Compiled by Shaykh al-Saduq in *Al-Khisal*, this hadith highlights the principle that divine acceptance of supplication is contingent upon the condition of human effort (*asbab*), illustrating the synergy between prayer and action. It specifically addresses social, financial, and physical negligence, such as a husband retaining a difficult wife despite having the means to divorce her or a lender failing to secure a witness, emphasizing that du'a without practical steps is incomplete.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 5-72 Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutevakil - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ali al-Kufy and Muhammad ibn al-Hussein, on the authority of Muhammad ibn of Ahmad ibn Muhammad, on the authority of Himad al-Harithi, on the authority of Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) that God’s Prophet (MGB) said, “The supplications of five people will not be answered: a man whose wife bothers him and he doesn’t divorce her, even though he can pay the expenses of divorcing her; a man whose slave has escaped three times, but still he doesn’t sell him; a man who passes by a semi-broken down wall and the wall falls upon him, and he doesn’t escape; a man who has given a loan to another one, and has not taken anyone as a witness for it; and a man who sits in his house and says, ‘O God! Please grant my daily bread!’ and who does not go to work.’
